    Glossary

    Definitions marked TBD are still to be written. Tracked in issue #26.

    Permissive license
    A license, such as BSD or MIT, that allows you to use, modify, and redistribute the code with little restriction. It leaves no proprietary control to the original owner.
    Copyleft license
    A license that requires any modified or unmodified code you redistribute to be licensed under the same form of license. The University of California (UC) calls these licenses “hereditary”. They are sometimes called “viral”.
    Hereditary
    UC’s term for a copyleft license. Refer to copyleft license.
    Patent-granting license
    A license that grants users a license to the copyrights in the code and also gives all later users rights to any patent of the licensor that the code needs, including patents the licensor gets in the future. GPL 3.0 and Apache 2.0 are examples.
    Delegated authority
    At UC, the campus office that can approve open source licensing of work the Regents own. It is usually the campus technology licensing, copyright, or patent office. UC’s guidance on the risk of each license is advice only. The delegated authority approves every case.
    Dual licensing
    Releasing the same software under two different licenses. It needs the agreement of all authors and, where campus rules require it, the delegated authority.
    Public domain
    Work that no one holds exclusive rights to, so anyone may use it for any purpose. It is not a license. A creator can choose to dedicate a work to the public domain, as the tz database project did. The rules differ between countries, so ask your campus office before you use a public domain dedication.
    Copyright
    Applies to original works of authorship. It protects the expression of an idea, but not the idea itself. It applies automatically and does not require a © notice. The copyright owner has the exclusive right to copy, distribute, modify, perform, and display the work.
    Patent
    Applies to inventions. An invention must meet five criteria: patentable subject matter, utility, novelty, non-obviousness, and enablement. A patent is not automatic: the inventor must apply for one. A patent gives the right to use, make, sell, offer for sale, and import.
    License
    Permission from the copyright or patent owner to use, copy, distribute, make, or sell the work or invention. The owner can set restrictions or obligations on use in the license.
    Open source license
    A license that is royalty-free and permits the licensee to use, copy, modify, and distribute the software. The source code is made available to end users so they can exercise those rights.
    Royalty-free
    End users do not pay any money.
    Licensee
    The end user, who is permitted to use, copy, modify, and distribute the software.
    Strong copyleft
    A copyleft license at the far end of the spectrum from permissive licenses. GPL 2.0 is an example: it requires your code to be placed under the terms of the GPL.
    Weak copyleft
    A copyleft license that typically limits either the scope of what counts as a derivative work, or the trigger for the copyleft provision. For example, the LGPL may allow you to dynamically link to an LGPL library without triggering the copyleft provision.
    Tech Transfer office (TTO)
    The campus office you check with before you release code under an open source license. It is sometimes called the Office of Intellectual Property or Technology Commercialization. It verifies ownership and funding requirements, makes sure no third-party restrictions apply, and helps you select a license from the UC-recommended list. In UC guidance this office is usually the delegated authority. Refer to delegated authority.
    The Regents of the University of California
    At UC, the typical owner of software created using university resources, or in connection with a research project or a staff position.
    Intellectual property (IP)
    A general term referring to intangible creations of human intellect. The types most often associated with software are copyright, patents, and trademarks.
    Trademark
    A sign, design, or expression that identifies products or services from a particular source, for example your software, as distinguished from other sources.
    Work for hire
    Work you create as part of your job. Often the employer owns the copyright in such work. If your employer owns the copyright, you probably have to get formal permission to license and distribute your software.
    Proprietary license
    Also called a closed-source license. It typically conveys rights to use the software but reserves the rights to access or distribute the source code.
    Dependency
    TBD
    License compatibility
    TBD
    OSI-approved
    A license that the Open Source Initiative (OSI) has assessed and judged to qualify as “open source”. The primary mission of the OSI is to assess licenses and maintain a list of those that qualify.
    COSS
    Commercial open source software. Software that a business releases under an open source license while it earns money from something it does not give away, such as enterprise features, a hosted service, or support. Open source is the business’s strategy, not its business model.

    Derivative work
    For software, a derivative work amounts to modifications to someone else’s software.
    Enjoined
    TBD
    All Rights Reserved
    The default when you do not specify a license for your software: all rights in the software are reserved to the copyright owner. It is also common to see “All rights reserved” stated explicitly as a form of license.

    Sources

    The definition of COSS follows the discussion in the UC Open 2026 panel Making a COSS Play (chaired by Karla Padilla), reworded by the lesson authors. Karla is asked to confirm the wording.

    The definitions of permissive license, copyleft license, hereditary, patent-granting license, delegated authority, and dual licensing are adapted from the University of California Office of the President’s guidance on open source software:

    • OSS Chart Companion (2018)
    • Guide to Managing Open Source Software at UC (2018)
    • OSS Chart (2018)

    The definitions of copyright, patent, license, open source license, royalty-free, licensee, strong copyleft, weak copyleft, Tech Transfer office, and The Regents of the University of California are adapted from the 2026 OSPO licensing presentation used in this lesson.

    The definitions of OSI-approved, derivative work, All Rights Reserved, intellectual property, trademark, work for hire, and proprietary license are adapted from Software Licensing by David E. Bernholdt, Lauren E. Milechin, Dave Rumph, Michael A. Heroux, and James Willenbring (INTERSECT), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Changes: shortened and lightly reworded.
